**Proof.**

We want to find an integer $n$ such that every integer in the block $\{n, n+1, \dots, n+1000000\}$ has a square factor greater than $1$, i.e. is **not** squarefree.

**Construction via the Chinese Remainder Theorem.**

Select $1000001$ distinct primes
$$p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{1000000}.$$
(There are infinitely many primes, so this is possible.)

For each $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, 1000000\}$, impose the congruence
$$n \equiv -i \pmod{p_i^2}.$$
Equivalently, $n + i \equiv 0 \pmod{p_i^2}$, so $p_i^2 \mid (n+i)$.

Since the primes $p_0, \dots, p_{1000000}$ are distinct, the moduli $p_0^2, p_1^2, \dots, p_{1000000}^2$ are pairwise coprime. By the **Chinese Remainder Theorem**, the system of congruences
$$n \equiv -i \pmod{p_i^2}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \dots, 1000000,$$
has a solution $n$ (in fact a unique residue class modulo $\prod_{i=0}^{1000000} p_i^2$).

**Verification.** For this $n$, each $n+i$ ($0 \le i \le 1000000$) is divisible by $p_i^2 > 1$, hence has a square factor greater than $1$. Therefore $\mu(n+i) = 0$ for every $i = 0, 1, \dots, 1000000$.

**Conclusion.** Such an integer $n$ exists. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE

So we need 1000001 consecutive integers all having a square factor > 1 (i.e., none of them is squarefree).

This is a classic application of the Chinese Remainder Theorem. We want to find n such that each n+i for i=0,...,1000000 is divisible by some p_i^2 where p_i are distinct primes.

Choose distinct primes p_0, p_1, ..., p_{1000000}. For each i, require n + i ≡ 0 (mod p_i^2), i.e., n ≡ -i (mod p_i^2).

By CRT (since p_i^2 are pairwise coprime as p_i are distinct primes), there exists a solution n modulo the product. So such n exists.
